chapter: Streetcar, Cab revival shows and trips abroad
title: Murray Wanger's Cotton Club revue in Miami and Cab's disastrous rehearsals
summary: Manager Murray Wanger wanted to recreate a Cotton Club show in Miami. Barefield assembled the band and wrote the music, then conducted opening night when Cab was disgusted by the confusion, and the show was a hit.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: And then in '57 Cab -- this -- let's see, how was that? Oh, Murray Wanger, do you know that name? Well, he was the man that -- that managed Mae West, managed a lot of big movie stars. This guy, he was a marvelous manager, and he made three or four fortunes in managing. And he was a spender. He was a great money spender.

He got an idea to recreate a Cotton Club show on the beach in Miami. So he contacted Cab, and Cab told him to get in touch with me. So he got in touch with me. And we got together to put a band together for this show and get the music together. So I became the musical director.
We used -- let's see, we used three trumpets, one trombone and four saxes and three rhythms. In fact, I had Herbie Jones on trumpet. Who were the --
(Inaudible) Cotton Club Review with dancers and --

Yes, it was the whole thing, just like the old Cotton Club, chorus girls, yeah. So anyway I put this band together and made -- and got the music and made the arrangements. Ben Davis was the composer of a lot of music, Benny Davis. He wrote a lot of music for the old Cotton Club.
And so I started, made these arrangmeents. We had jungle numbers and all this. And so I told the guy, I said,

Murray, I said -- he just wanted to know how much it would be. I said, 'Well, you got to pay the guys so much, whatever the scale was, you got to pay them so much.' And for myself, I said, I'll go down. You know, he was short of money. So he said, 'What can you do?' I said, well, 'I'll put the band together, but the men will have to get paid. If you -- I'll go down and rehearse, you know, went to Miami a week ahead of time, and I'll write the music and rehearse the band, and when it is finished, you pay me for the music and I'll come on back to New York,' because Cab was there, you know.

So anyway, we went -- I put this band together, three trumpets, one trombone, four saxes and rhythms, three rhythms, and we went to Miami, and I said, the guys have got to get a week's salary for the week that we're there rehearsing. Well, I sat down, and I didn't even go to rehearsal. I just sat and wrote the music and sent it out to rehearsal, and Cab rehearsed the band. And they put this show together.

Well, opening night we go out there and the place -- this was a big, barny place, great big place, and the place was packed with people. And Cab was so disgusted, you know. He says, 'Put on a tuxedo and conduct the show.' I said, 'Well, I don't know what you've been doing.' Just, he said -- I said okay. 'Just write me a routine.' I knew the music. 'Write me a routine of the show.' So they wrote me a routine of the show,

and I put on a tuxedo and went in there and conducted the show, because everybody was so disgusted with the -- we never did get through a dress rehearsal that day. They never did get through a dress rehearsal, so I had to -- so we ran that show down, and when they ended the show, the audience was standing up screaming.

So now I go to Murray. I says, 'well, the show's on. I can go back to New York.' He says, 'No, I want you to stay and conduct the show.' So I stayed there and conducted the show, and this show was a big hit. I mean everybody -- so now Murray Wanger wanted to -- it was so big that he had a place next door in a much more fabulous building he wanted to put this show in. So he started getting this building ready to put this show in and move. And he told me.
